Just now

--

Adding a generative chatbot to a tool whose whole promise is determinism would have refuted the argument. Here is what I built instead.
Every product I touch this year seems to be growing a chatbot. So when the idea came up for ArchPatterns, my free architecture pattern selector, the obvious move was to add one too: a little assistant in the corner you could ask “which pattern should I use?”
I decided not to. Deliberately, and I think correctly. Here is the reasoning, because it goes to the heart of what the tool is for.
The thing ArchPatterns offers is determinism
ArchPatterns is rule-based. You answer a short wizard about the solution you are shaping, and it recommends candidate archetypes, the design patterns that support them, and the anti-patterns your answers put you at risk of, with the reasoning shown for every recommendation. The same inputs always produce the same output. Every rule weight is inspectable. Nothing is generated on the fly.
That is not an accident of implementation. It is the entire proposition. An architect can take a recommendation into a design review and defend it, because it is reproducible and traceable, not the output of a model that might say something different tomorrow.
A generative chatbot is the exact opposite of all of that. It is non-deterministic, opaque, and capable of stating, with total confidence, that a pattern exists when it does not, or attributing it to the wrong source. Bolting one onto a tool whose whole promise is “no black box, every answer traceable” would not add a feature. It would quietly refute the argument.
But people still want to ask a question
The instinct behind “add a chatbot” is a real one, though. Not everyone wants to work through a structured wizard. Sometimes you just want to type “how do I handle failures between services?” and see what is relevant.
That is a retrieval problem, not a generation problem. And retrieval can be done deterministically.
So instead of a chatbot, I built something called Ask the library. You type your question in plain words. It ranks the entries by relevance and returns the real ones, with their real definitions and their real citations. There is no language model in the answer path. Nothing is written on the fly. It cannot invent a pattern, because it can only ever surface entries that already exist. Ask the same question twice and you get the same results.
It feels conversational. It is, under the hood, honest search. That distinction is the whole point.
Conversational access, done on the right side
There is a second, subtler reason I did not need an on-site chatbot: the conversational version already exists, just not hosted by me.
ArchPatterns exposes a Model Context Protocol server, which means an AI assistant can consult the library directly and get back deterministic, source-attributed entries. If you want to converse with the patterns, you can, from inside your own assistant. The generation happens on your side, clearly labelled as your assistant’s work, drawing on my tool’s structured, attributed data. My tool supplies the facts; your assistant supplies the conversation. The responsibilities stay where they belong, and my library never has to pretend to be something it is not.
The uncomfortable restraint
I want to be honest that Ask the library is not magic. It is keyword retrieval, not semantic understanding. Occasionally the single best entry for a query ranks a few places down from where you would put it. I tuned it to a point, and then I stopped, because closing that last gap would have meant reaching for either a hand-curated synonym map or an embedding model, and the latter reintroduces exactly the non-determinism I had chosen to avoid.
That trade, accepting slightly less clever ranking in exchange for a guarantee that nothing is ever invented, is the same trade the whole product makes. It is the trade I would want from any tool I was going to rely on in a serious decision.
Against the reflex
There is a reflex right now to treat “add generative AI” as self-evidently an upgrade. Sometimes it is. But for a tool whose job is to be a trustworthy reference, the reflex is worth resisting. The value of a reference is that it is correct and checkable. A feature that makes it occasionally, confidently wrong is not an upgrade to a reference. It is a downgrade wearing a fashionable coat.
So ArchPatterns has search, not a chatbot. You can ask it anything you like, in plain language, and everything it hands back is real. That felt like the version worth building.
It is free, and at archpatterns.io.
